title: Betz v. Commissioner
articleTitle: The Evolution of Substantiation Standards in Federal Research Tax Credits: A Comprehensive Analysis of Betz v. Commissioner
subject: Pilot Models and Documentation Standards
summary: Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84, is a U.S. Tax Court R&D tax credit case involving the S corporation shareholders of Catalytic Products International, a custom air pollution control system designer. The court denied all research credits for 2014 through 2016 and sustained 20% accuracy-related penalties, holding that custom commercial oxidizers were not pilot models and wage claims lacked substantiation.

body.text: Section 1: Executive Summary and Case Background
Factual Matrix and the Taxpayer's Claim

In the consolidated cases of Mark Betz and Christine Betz v. Commissioner and Dennis Lincoln and Julia Lincoln v. Commissioner, Docket Nos. 21587-18 and 21588-18, decided as Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84 (filed July 6, 2023), the United States Tax Court addressed a sweeping dispute regarding the substantiation and structural eligibility of federal research and development (R&D) tax credits claimed under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) § 41. The petitioners, Mark and Christine Betz alongside Dennis and Julia Lincoln, were the two groups of joint filers that included the sole shareholders of Catalytic Products International, Inc. (CPI)—Mark Betz and Julia Lincoln, who each owned 50% of the shares—an S corporation founded in 1969 by Erwin Betz and engaged in the design and supply of custom-built industrial air pollution control systems, primarily catalytic and thermal oxidizers, with the physical fabrication and assembly of the systems performed by third-party subcontractors rather than by CPI itself. In its normal course of business, CPI engineered these pollution abatement systems to satisfy specific customer site parameters and emissions requirements, routinely purchasing fabricated components from third-party vendors and engaging external subcontractors (typically PRE-Heat, Inc.) to fabricate and assemble the final units at the subcontractors' facilities, after which the units were shipped to client facilities for installation by CPI, the customer, or a third-party contractor.

Following an engagement with the third-party tax advisory firm alliantgroup, CPI claimed a federal credit for increasing research activities of $501,531 on its 2014 Form 1120S, U.S. Income Tax Return for an S Corporation, spanning 19 commercial customer projects. Because CPI operated as a pass-through entity under Subchapter S of the Internal Revenue Code, the claimed credits flowed through to the individual shareholders on their respective Forms 1040, generating both immediate tax offsets in 2014 and unused research credit carryforwards applied to the 2015 and 2016 tax years. The $501,531 credit calculation rested on two primary categories of Qualified Research Expenses (QREs) under IRC § 41(b): internal employee wages—including substantial compensation paid to CPI's vice president of engineering (petitioner Mark Betz) and vice president of sales (Robert Shaver), whose wages Alliantgroup allocated evenly across all 19 projects and which accounted for roughly 59% of the $1,983,647 in claimed wage QREs, as well as engineers, draftsmen, project managers, and sales engineers—and $5,732,211 of supply expenditures consisting of amounts paid to suppliers and subcontractors for fabricating, assembling, and supplying the components of the custom-built systems (supply costs were claimed for 18 of the 19 projects, with none claimed for the DuPont La Porte project), which the taxpayers' pretrial memorandum characterized in their entirety as experimental "pilot models".
The Internal Revenue Service Challenge and Procedural Posture

Following an examination of the returns, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) issued statutory notices of deficiency disallowing 100% of the claimed research credits across all 19 projects for the 2014 tax year, eliminating the resultant credit carryforwards for 2015 and 2016, and assessing 20% accuracy-related penalties under IRC § 6662(a) for negligence and substantial understatements of income tax. The Commissioner challenged the claims on multiple cascading fronts. First, the IRS contended that CPI engaged in routine custom engineering and commercial adaptation rather than resolving objective technological uncertainty under IRC § 174. Second, the IRS argued that the 19 air pollution control units were final commercial products built for customer sale rather than experimental pilot models under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4), thereby disqualifying all claimed supply QREs. Third, the Service asserted that the taxpayers failed to substantiate that employee wages were incurred in the performance of qualified services under IRC § 41(b)(2), objecting to the consultant's reliance on retrospective interviews and unsupported percentage allocations. Finally, the IRS maintained that several of the underlying customer contracts transferred ownership or restricted the use of the technical outputs, rendering the work excluded "funded research" under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H).
Governing Statutory and Regulatory Framework

To evaluate CPI's claims within the United States federal tax jurisdiction, Judge Nega applied the interlocking statutory provisions of IRC §§ 41, 174, 6001, 6662, and 6664, alongside their corresponding Treasury Regulations. Under IRC § 41(a) and § 41(b), a taxpayer may claim a credit based on qualified research expenses—restricted to in-house research expenses (wages paid for qualified services and supplies used in the conduct of qualified research) and contract research expenses—incurred in carrying on a trade or business. For an activity to constitute "qualified research" under IRC § 41(d)(1), the taxpayer bears the affirmative burden of proving under Tax Court Rule 142(a) and Welch v. Helvering, 290 U.S. 111 (1933), that each distinct business component satisfies a cumulative four-part statutory test.

The first element of this statutory framework is the Section 174 Threshold Test under IRC § 41(d)(1)(A), which mandates that expenditures be eligible for treatment as research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174 as applicable to the 2014 tax year. While the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 subsequently mandated capitalization under IRC § 174 beginning in 2022 and 2025 federal legislation enacted IRC § 174A to restore domestic current deductibility for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, the underlying substantive definition of research expenditures in Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2 remains the foundational threshold for credit eligibility. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1), expenditures qualify only if incurred in the experimental or laboratory sense to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the capability, method, or appropriate design for developing or improving a product. Furthermore, under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4), the costs of producing a physical product qualify only if the unit constitutes a "pilot model"—defined as any representation or model of a product that is produced to evaluate and resolve uncertainty concerning the product during its development or improvement.

The second statutory pillar is the Technological in Nature Test under IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i), which requires that the research be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature, necessitating reliance on the principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. This links directly to the third requirement, the Business Component and Permitted Purpose Test under IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and § 41(d)(3)(A), under which the taxpayer must intend that the discovered information be useful in the development of a new or improved business component—defined as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used in the taxpayer's trade or business—for a permitted purpose, specifically a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality. Finally, the fourth requirement is the Process of Experimentation and "Substantially All" Test under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C), which dictates that substantially all of the research activities—defined by Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6) as at least 80% of a business component's research activities measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis—must constitute elements of a process of experimentation involving the identification of uncertainty, the identification of alternatives, and a systematic evaluative process (such as modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error) consistent with the scientific method.

If an overall product fails the four-part test at the macro level, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) mandates the application of the "shrinking-back" rule, under which the four-part test is reapplied to progressively smaller subsets, components, or subcomponents until either a qualifying subcomponent is isolated or the most basic level of the product fails to satisfy the requirements. Even if the four-part test is satisfied, the activity must not fall within the statutory exclusions of IRC § 41(d)(4), most notably the adaptation exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) (activities adapting an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need) and the funded research exclusion under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) (research funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person where the taxpayer fails to retain substantial rights or bears no financial risk of research failure).
Final Judicial Holding and Second-Order Tax Implications

In a comprehensive memorandum opinion, the Tax Court sustained the Commissioner's determinations in full, holding that the taxpayers were entitled to zero research tax credits for 2014, 2015, and 2016, and were personally liable for accuracy-related penalties under IRC § 6662(a) across all three years. Specifically, Judge Nega held that for all 19 projects, the taxpayers failed to establish that the custom-built air pollution control systems were pilot models under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4), eliminating all claimed supply QREs. The Court further held that for all 19 projects, the taxpayers failed to prove that any employee wages were incurred in the performance of qualified services under IRC § 41(b)(2)—in most instances because CPI already possessed the information establishing each system's basic design specification (often before 2014), and in the few instances where the Court did find investigative activities (e.g., the Akzo Nobel flame arrestor meeting, the Celanese gas train inquiry, the Smalley furnace testing, and the East Balt airflow measurements) because those activities were not shown to be part of a process of experimentation or the record failed to identify the employees who performed them, leaving no reasonable basis for a Cohan estimate—eliminating all wage QREs. Additionally, for five of the eight customer contracts specifically examined for funded research, CPI retained only incidental benefits and lacked substantial rights in the research results, disqualifying those projects independently under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H). Finally, the Court held that the taxpayers had abandoned any reasonable cause and good faith defense under IRC § 6664(c) by failing to argue it in their posttrial briefing and, in the alternative, that any apparent reliance on their third-party R&D tax consultant, Alliantgroup, was inconsistent with ordinary business care and prudence, so the Section 6662 penalties were sustained.

Beyond the immediate disallowance, Betz v. Commissioner establishes critical second- and third-order legal benchmarks for the technical tax community. First, the decision demonstrates how a taxpayer's aggressive macro-level business component definition—claiming an entire commercial machine as a single business component to capture 100% of material fabrication costs as "pilot model" supplies—creates a catastrophic evidentiary trap. When the macro unit fails the Section 174 uncertainty test because the information establishing its basic design specification (destruction efficiency, airflow volume, and the VOCs at issue) was already available to the taxpayer—often before the credit year—the absence of evidence identifying the specific investigative activities, the employees who performed them, and their associated costs at the subcomponent level prevents the court from meaningfully applying the Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) shrinking-back rule, resulting in a total forfeiture of any potentially qualifying subcomponent activities. Second, aligned closely with the Seventh Circuit's opinion in Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), Betz underscores that custom-engineered-to-order (ETO) manufacturers cannot conflate project-specific configuration, site integration, or post-production acceptance testing with a scientific process of experimentation.
Section 2: Core Legal and Evidentiary Failures
Absence of Objective Technological Uncertainty and the Economic Irrationality Standard

The foundational collapse of the taxpayers' claim in Betz occurred at the very first statutory hurdle: the Section 174 uncertainty test incorporated via IRC § 41(d)(1)(A). Under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1), uncertainty exists only if the information objectively available to the taxpayer does not establish the capability or method for developing or improving the product, or the appropriate design of the product. The petitioners contended that because each catalytic or thermal oxidizer was custom-engineered for a specific industrial application, the appropriate design of the oxidizer as a whole remained uncertain until the completed system was installed at the customer's facility and successfully passed onsite emissions and performance testing.

Judge Nega dismantled this argument by cross-examining the taxpayers' assertions against CPI's contemporaneous commercial records and business conduct. The evidentiary record revealed that CPI's project proposals—many of which were accepted by customers in 2013—already memorialized the basic design specification of the oxidizers (type of oxidizer, airflow volume, VOCs at issue, and guaranteed destruction efficiency), so that any investigative activities relating to the oxidizers as a whole were performed, and the corresponding wages incurred, in 2013 rather than in the 2014 credit year. Furthermore, in multiple instances, CPI had previously designed and supplied (through subcontracted fabrication) oxidizer or related systems to the exact same customers (e.g., Isola, Mitsubishi, Reclaimed Energy, and Intel). The Court emphasized that performing routine engineering calculations on already-available thermodynamic or airflow data to size equipment, or engaging a third-party subcontractor to build a component to a customer's provided specifications, does not constitute an investigative activity intended to discover technological information. Echoing the Seventh Circuit's admonition in Little Sandy Coal, the Court distinguished genuine technological uncertainty from the generic uncertainty inherent in any manufacturing or construction endeavor—where engineers must determine exact dimensions, select appropriate fasteners, or verify component fitment using established engineering methodologies.

Crucially, the Tax Court articulated an "economic irrationality" standard to refute the taxpayers' claim that system-wide design uncertainty persisted until final onsite testing. The Court observed that throughout the 19 projects, CPI routinely committed substantial capital early in the project lifecycle to purchase custom-sized, high-value components from third-party suppliers and paid subcontractors for full-scale fabrication long before any onsite testing occurred. Judge Nega concluded that incurring such massive upfront material and fabrication expenses would be economically irrational if CPI genuinely lacked information establishing the appropriate design of the oxidizer as a whole. As for the post-installation testing at the customer's site, the Court held that such evaluations did not establish that the appropriate design of an oxidizer as a whole remained uncertain until the tests were completed, and that specific testing such as the dye penetrant testing on the Teva project and the postinstallation testing on the Isola II project constituted excluded quality control testing under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(6)(i) and (a)(7)—which encompasses testing or inspection to determine whether particular units of materials or products conform to specified parameters—rather than experimental testing undertaken to validate a design hypothesis or resolve fundamental design uncertainty.
Misapplication of the Pilot Model Exception and Disallowance of Supply QREs

Directly tied to the Section 174 uncertainty failure was CPI's improper classification of its commercial inventory and production costs as supply QREs under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4). Under the regulations, expenditures for the acquisition or production of depreciable property are barred from Section 174 treatment, and routine commercial production costs do not qualify as research supplies; however, the tangible costs of constructing a "pilot model" qualify as deductible Section 174 expenditures (and consequently as Section 41 supply QREs) if the model is produced specifically to evaluate and resolve technological uncertainty concerning the product during its development or improvement.

In their pretrial memorandum (though not explicitly in their posttrial briefing), the taxpayers asserted that each of the custom-built oxidizers for which supply costs were claimed constituted a "pilot model" merely because each system was uniquely configured for a particular customer application and underwent post-construction testing. The Tax Court rejected this contention across all 19 projects, ruling that uniqueness or one-off customization does not transform a commercial end-product into an experimental prototype. Examining the purchasing invoices, customer contracts, and subcontractor agreements, the Court determined that CPI's suppliers and subcontractors were not constructing experimental representations or scale models to test competing design alternatives; rather, they were fabricating the final, commercial-grade oxidizer units ordered by CPI's customers for permanent industrial operation. Because CPI's primary purpose in constructing the 19 units was to fulfill commercial sales orders rather than to resolve developmental uncertainty, 100% of the claimed supply QREs were disallowed.
Triggering the Adaptation Exclusion in Custom Engineering Environments

In addition to failing the affirmative Section 174 uncertainty threshold, CPI's activities on at least one project ran squarely into the statutory adaptation exclusion of IRC § 41(d)(4)(B), which the Court applied as an alternative holding. Under IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(3) (illustrated in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(10)), qualified research expressly excludes any activity related to the adaptation of an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need. While the regulatory preamble to T.D. 8930 clarifies that the adaptation exclusion does not independently disqualify an activity that otherwise satisfies the four-part test by resolving genuine technological uncertainty, Betz illustrates how the Tax Court utilizes the adaptation exclusion as an alternative ground to reinforce disallowance when a custom manufacturer essentially replicates a preexisting design.

A prime illustration analyzed by the Court was CPI's "M&W Ireland" project. Although the taxpayers claimed the M&W Ireland system involved qualified research, the accepted proposal for this ammonium fluoride wastewater treatment system (a TRIMIX system combining an air stripper with a catalytic oxidizer) for an Intel facility in Leixlip, Ireland stated that CPI would provide an exact copy of the TRIMIX system it had recently completed for Intel, requiring only minor site-specific modifications—chiefly substituting European components that met CE product standards and making corresponding sizing adjustments—to accommodate the client's specific installation site. Having first held that the information from CPI's prior Intel project established the basic design specification and that no investigative activities were shown, the Court held in the alternative (n. 44) that an exact copy of a previous product with some minor site-specific modifications falls squarely within the plain meaning of the exclusion; in conforming an established product architecture to a customer's site and European product-standard requirements, CPI was merely adapting an existing business component within the explicit prohibition of IRC § 41(d)(4)(B).
Failure to Substantiate Process of Experimentation, Wage QREs, and the Shrinking-Back Rule

Even where isolated technical challenges may have arisen within specific subassemblies of the 19 oxidizers, the taxpayers failed to satisfy the Process of Experimentation requirement of IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and the wage substantiation mandate of IRC § 41(b)(2). Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C), at least 80% of a business component's research activities must constitute elements of a process of experimentation capable of evaluating more than one alternative to achieve a result where the capability, method, or appropriate design is uncertain. The Tax Court held that even where CPI employees performed some investigative activities—such as the February 2014 Akzo Nobel meeting regarding the flame arrestor, Mr. Betz's email to a burner supplier regarding the Celanese gas train, and contacting suppliers for the DuPont La Porte custom burner—those activities were not part of a structured process of experimentation requiring use of the scientific method, and, with respect to the Smalley furnace testing, the taxpayers failed to establish a methodical plan constituting a process of experimentation.

Furthermore, the Court recognized the legal possibility that even though the 19 oxidizers failed the four-part test as complete systems, specific wages or component supplies might have qualified at the component or subcomponent level through the "shrinking-back" rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2). Similarly, under the Seventh Circuit's controlling precedent in Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023)—which Judge Nega cited extensively throughout Betz—a taxpayer that fails to document research activities corresponding to project subcomponents cannot invoke the shrinking-back rule, and shortcut estimates of experimentation-related activities will not suffice; notably, Betz itself did not reach the computation of the 80% substantially-all fraction or the treatment of direct supervision and direct support under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B), resolving the wage claims instead under the Section 174 test, the process of experimentation requirement (as an alternative holding), and the Cohan doctrine. However, CPI's evidentiary record suffered from a fatal structural flaw: the alliantgroup credit study designated each entire oxidizer system as a single monolithic business component and aggregated all project hours and supply costs at the macro project level. Because the taxpayers provided zero documentation segregating uncertainties, experimental iterations, employee hours, or material costs by discrete subcomponent (such as an experimental catalytic bed geometry or a novel burner nozzle control loop), the Tax Court—although it undertook a shrinking-back inquiry for the sake of completeness to the extent the limited record allowed—was unable to bridge the evidentiary gap and apply the shrinking-back rule to any component.
Evidentiary Deficiencies, Retrospective Estimates, and the Inapplicability of the Cohan Doctrine

Under IRC § 6001 and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d), a taxpayer claiming a credit under IRC § 41 must retain records in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit. In Betz, CPI maintained no contemporaneous time-tracking system linking employee hours to specific research activities or subcomponents. Instead, to quantify wage QREs for engineers as well as high-level executives—specifically CPI's vice president of engineering (Mr. Betz) and vice president of sales (Mr. Shaver)—the taxpayers relied on retrospective percentage allocations that alliantgroup derived from interviews of Messrs. Betz and Harmsen conducted during an April 8, 2015 site visit, after the 2014 tax year had closed, supplemented at trial by witness testimony.

Judge Nega rejected the wage claims in their entirety, characterizing the petitioners' trial testimony as "vague, in conflict with the record, and lacking in credibility with respect to their self-serving characterizations of some of the work performed by CPI on specific projects". With respect to Messrs. Betz and Shaver—whose wages alliantgroup allocated evenly across all 19 projects and which made up roughly 59% of the claimed wage QREs—the record lacked any credible evidence proving that these executives personally performed qualified research, directly supervised specific experimental activities, or provided direct support rather than performing general executive management and administrative oversight.

In a last-ditch effort to salvage partial wage QREs, the petitioners urged the Court to estimate allowable research expenses under the longstanding judicial doctrine of Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930). While the Tax Court acknowledged that Cohan has not been universally abolished in R&D tax credit jurisprudence, it emphasized the strict prerequisite established in cases such as Eustace v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2001-66, and Little Sandy Coal: a court may estimate the quantitative amount of a deductible or creditable expense under Cohan only after the taxpayer has first proven actual entitlement to the credit by establishing that qualified research occurred, and only if the taxpayer provides a rational evidentiary basis upon which to ground an estimate. Because CPI failed to prove that any employee performed qualified services and offered only uncorroborated percentage allocations, failing even to identify which employees performed the few activities the Court found investigative, the Court refused to apply Cohan.
Disqualification Under the Funded Research Exclusion and Loss of Substantial Rights

Independent of the technological and substantiation failures, the Tax Court analyzed eight of the 19 project contracts under the funded research exclusion of IRC § 41(d)(4)(H), as a discrete alternative holding confined to the substantial rights prong that the Commissioner challenged. Under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1), research performed for another person under a contract is excluded as "funded research" unless the taxpayer both bears the financial risk of failure (meaning payment is contingent on the technical success of the research, per Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995), and Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015)) and retains "substantial rights" in the research results, per Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000), and Tangel v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-1.

Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2) and (3), a taxpayer does not retain substantial rights if the agreement confers on another person the exclusive right to exploit the results of the research or if the taxpayer must pay for the right to use the research results, and, under Tangel and Dynetics, Inc. v. United States, 121 Fed. Cl. 492 (2015), a contract requiring the taxpayer to obtain the customer's consent—with no conditions limiting the customer's ability to withhold it—before using the research results likewise leaves the taxpayer without substantial rights. Crucially, the regulation explicitly states that "incidental benefits to the taxpayer from performance of the research (for example, increased experience in a field of research) do not constitute substantial rights in the research". Reviewing the express terms and conditions of the customer agreements, Judge Nega held that for five of the eight analyzed projects (3M Hutchinson, 3M Hartford, 3M Monrovia, Celanese, and Enterprise—whereas CPI was held to retain substantial rights under the Smalley, Teva, and HA International contracts), the governing contracts either vested intellectual property and design rights exclusively in the customers or prohibited CPI from reusing the project designs and technical findings without authorization, leaving CPI with nothing more than incidental engineering experience. Consequently, all expenditures associated with those five projects were statutorily barred as funded research.
Imposition of Section 6662 Accuracy-Related Penalties and Collapse of the Consultant Reliance Defense

Finally, the Tax Court upheld 20% accuracy-related penalties under IRC § 6662(a) and (b)(1)–(2) for tax years 2014, 2015, and 2016 based on negligence (defined under IRC § 6662(c) and Treas. Reg. § 1.6662-3(b)(1) as any failure to make a reasonable attempt to comply with the provisions of the internal revenue laws, including the failure to keep adequate books and records or to substantiate items properly) and substantial understatements of income tax.

Although the affirmative defense of reasonable cause and good faith under IRC § 6664(c)(1) was potentially available to the petitioners—for example, through reliance on the professional advice of alliantgroup, which prepared the R&D tax credit study—the petitioners did not argue that defense in their posttrial briefing, offering only a single proposed finding that they were not liable for the penalties with a citation to the entire record, and they expressly stipulated that they did not rely on their return preparer, Porte Brown LLC, in claiming the research credit. To establish good-faith reliance on a professional tax advisor under Neonatology Associates, P.A. v. Commissioner, 115 T.C. 43 (2000), and Treas. Reg. § 1.6664-4(c), a taxpayer must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that the advisor was a competent professional with sufficient expertise to justify reliance, that the taxpayer provided necessary and accurate information to the advisor, and that the taxpayer actually relied in good faith on the advisor's judgment.

In Betz (specifically addressed at *113, n. 53), Judge Nega held that the petitioners had abandoned the reasonable cause defense by failing to raise it on brief and, in the alternative, rejected the petitioners' reliance defense. While later Tax Court jurisprudence—most notably George v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-10—clarified that the Court has not established a per se rule that reliance on alliantgroup can never be in good faith (finding reasonable reliance in George, where the consultant had extensive experience, had access to the company's data, and prepared a study of nearly 100 pages), the reliance defense in Betz failed because it was never properly raised and, alternatively, because any apparent reliance on alliantgroup was inconsistent with ordinary business care and prudence. Separately, the Court found the petitioners negligent because they failed to maintain adequate records substantiating their entitlement to the research credits under IRC § 6001 and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d)—a statutory recordkeeping duty that cannot be outsourced to a third-party study provider.
Section 3: Comparative Summary Table of Statutory Requirements and Evidentiary Standards

The following table maps each statutory and regulatory requirement adjudicated in Betz v. Commissioner against the specific evidentiary and structural failures of the taxpayer and the governing legal standard of proof enforced by the United States Tax Court.

cells: Section 174 Uncertainty Threshold: Expenditures must be incurred to discover information that eliminates objective uncertainty regarding capability, method, or appropriate product design.

Claimed design uncertainty existed across all 19 oxidizer systems until post-installation onsite testing passed. Failed because project proposals (many accepted in 2013) contained detailed design specs upfront, prior similar systems had been built for the same clients, and routine engineering calculations were used.

Taxpayer must prove objective lack of capability, method, or design information at project outset. Incurring high upfront component fabrication costs prior to testing is "economically irrational" if the overall design is genuinely uncertain.
Exclusion of Quality Control Testing: Testing or inspection to verify that units conform to specified parameters is excluded from Section 174 research.
Relied on post-production onsite commissioning and emissions verification testing at customer facilities as proof that the oxidizer design was experimental.
Post-production verification testing merely confirms conformance with predetermined customer specifications; it does not retroactively prove that design uncertainty existed during fabrication.

Pilot Model Exception (Supply QREs): Supply costs for constructing a physical product qualify only if the unit is a representation or model produced specifically to evaluate and resolve product design uncertainty.

Claimed 100% of the $5,732,211 in material and subcontracted construction costs for the custom oxidizers (18 of the 19 projects; none for DuPont La Porte) as "pilot models" based on their one-off customization for specific clients.

Disallowed 100% of supply QREs. Custom commercial end-products built to fulfill customer purchase orders are not experimental prototypes. Taxpayer must prove the primary purpose of construction was resolving technical uncertainty.
Adaptation Exclusion: Excludes activities that adapt an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement or need.

Claimed custom engineering on projects like "M&W Ireland," whose accepted proposal promised an exact copy of a TRIMIX wastewater treatment system recently supplied to Intel, with minor site-specific modifications (e.g., CE-compliant European components).

As an alternative holding (n. 44), an exact copy of a previous product with some minor site-specific modifications falls squarely within the plain meaning of the exclusion; conforming a preexisting product architecture to a customer's site parameters using known engineering methods is statutorily excluded adaptation.

Process of Experimentation & 80% "Substantially All" Rule: At least 80% of research activities (by cost or time) must constitute elements of a structured scientific process evaluating alternatives to resolve uncertainty.
Offered vague testimony regarding custom design iterations without test plans, documented hypotheses, modeling logs, or quantitative tracking of experimental vs. routine engineering time.

Requires concrete contemporaneous proof of a systematic evaluative process (hypothesis formulation, alternative modeling/simulation, systematic trial-and-error testing, and data analysis) accounting for of activities.
Shrinking-Back Rule: If a macro product fails the four-part test, the test applies to progressively smaller components or subcomponents until a qualifying subset is reached.
Defined each entire oxidizer unit as a single monolithic business component without segregating subcomponent uncertainties, engineering hours, or material costs.
The Court cannot manufacture subcomponent-level evidence. To invoke shrink-back, the taxpayer must maintain modular cost and time accounting mapped directly to discrete, uncertain subcomponents.
Qualified Services (Wage QREs): Wages must be paid for engaging in qualified research, or direct supervision / direct support of qualified research.

Claimed percentage allocations of wages for engineers and executives (the Vice Presidents of Engineering and Sales) via retrospective interviews without linking specific tasks to experimental activities.

Disallowed 100% of wage QREs. Following Little Sandy Coal, shortcut estimates of experimentation-related activities will not suffice; the taxpayer must show that particular employees performed qualified services (or direct supervision/support of qualified research), and the Court declined any Cohan estimate absent that threshold showing.
IRC § 6001, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d) & Cohan Rule
Recordkeeping & Estimation Foundation: Taxpayer must retain usable records substantiating eligibility; Cohan estimation applies only after proving actual entitlement and a rational basis.
Relied on alliantgroup's retrospective employee interviews, arbitrary percentage estimates, and self-serving trial testimony that contradicted contemporaneous project documents.
Refused to apply Cohan v. Commissioner. Retrospective estimates and unsupported percentages cannot substitute for proof of underlying qualified research or cure a lack of initial entitlement.
Funded Research Exclusion: Research performed under contract is excluded unless the taxpayer bears financial risk of failure and retains "substantial rights" in the research results.
Claimed credits on customer contracts that assigned IP ownership to the client or barred CPI from reusing designs without client consent or fee payment.

Disqualified 5 of 8 analyzed contracts as funded research. Retaining general engineering know-how or field experience constitutes mere "incidental benefits," which Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2) excludes from substantial rights.
Accuracy-Related Penalties & Reasonable Cause: Imposes 20% penalty for negligence or substantial understatement unless taxpayer proves good-faith reliance on a fully informed advisor.

Did not argue reasonable cause in posttrial briefing (only a bare proposed finding of no penalty liability) and stipulated that they did not rely on their CPA return preparer, Porte Brown, in claiming the credit.

Sustained 20% penalties across 2014–2016 (*113, n. 53). Reasonable cause defense deemed abandoned; alternatively, any apparent reliance on alliantgroup was inconsistent with ordinary business care and prudence. Negligence established by the failure to maintain adequate records substantiating the credits.

body.text: Section 4: Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the judicial mandates of Betz v. Commissioner into actionable tax governance, the following two applied industry case studies examine engineering and manufacturing enterprises facing the exact statutory pitfalls that defeated CPI. Each case study provides a rigorous, step-by-step remedial protocol across project governance, technical documentation, contract structuring, and contemporaneous expense tracking.
Case Study 1: Custom Industrial Thermal and Abatement Equipment Manufacturer (Engineered-to-Order Hardware)
Baseline Scenario and Legal Pitfalls

AeroTherm Abatement Systems, Inc. (AeroTherm), a United States Subchapter S corporation based in Ohio, designs and manufactures custom Regenerative Thermal Oxidizers (RTOs) and ultra-high-temperature hydrogen combustion scrubbers for petrochemical refineries. In the current tax year, AeroTherm enters into a $4.2 million contract with a Gulf Coast refinery to deliver a custom RTO system capable of destroying 99.95% of halogenated volatile organic compounds (VOCs) in a corrosive, fluctuating exhaust stream while reducing supplemental natural gas consumption by 40%.

While 85% of the RTO system (the structural steel housing, standard centrifugal fans, ductwork, foundation skid, and standard PLC cabinets) utilizes well-established mechanical engineering and off-the-shelf components procured from third-party fabricators, AeroTherm's engineering team faces a genuine scientific challenge in one discrete subassembly: the Catalytic Ceramic Honeycomb Matrix and High-Cycle Rotary Valve Seal (Subcomponent C-4). Existing rotary valve seals warp under the thermal shock of halogenated acid gases at , and standard ceramic media suffer rapid catalytic poisoning.

Left unguided, AeroTherm's leadership intends to replicate the exact fatal errors committed in Betz. Specifically, management plans to define the entire $4.2 million commercial RTO unit as a single "Pilot Model" business component to claim $3.1 million in third-party structural steel and commercial fabrication invoices as supply QREs. Furthermore, the company intends to point to post-installation EPA Method 25A stack emissions testing at the refinery as proof that the entire RTO remained uncertain until final commissioning. Finally, AeroTherm plans to wait until year-end to have an external consultant interview the Vice President of Engineering and the Company President to estimate that 60% of all engineering and executive wages were spent on qualified research.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Protocol
Step 1: Project Governance and Subcomponent Business Component Architecture (Enabling Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2) Shrink-Back)

To neutralize the "economic irrationality" and macro-unit disallowance rules of Betz and Little Sandy Coal, AeroTherm must immediately abandon the macro-system business component claim and restructure its internal Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) and Project Lifecycle Management (PLM) governance prior to project kickoff. During the initial engineering gate review, AeroTherm's Chief Technology Officer and Tax Director formally partition the contract in the ERP system into two distinct accounting hierarchies. The first hierarchy, designated as Job Code 2026-RTO-100 (Commercial Balance of Plant - Non-Qualifying), captures all routine configuration, adaptation under IRC § 41(d)(4)(B), structural CAD drafting, vendor procurement, and site installation for the oxidizer housing, blowers, ductwork, and standard controls. The second hierarchy, designated as Job Code 2026-RTO-100-EXP-C4 (Subcomponent Business Component - Qualifying), isolates the Halogen-Resistant Rotary Valve Seal and Doped Ceramic Catalyst Subassembly as a standalone business component under IRC § 41(d)(2)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2).

Rather than procuring the full-scale commercial RTO and calling it a pilot model, AeroTherm authorizes a dedicated internal fabrication work order under Job Code 2026-RTO-100-EXP-C4 to build three scaled benchtop test rigs and sacrificial rotary seal assemblies in its Ohio test bay prior to releasing final commercial fabrication drawings to third-party suppliers. Because these three sacrificial seal rigs are never delivered to the customer, are destroyed during thermal cycling tests, and exist solely to resolve design uncertainty before commercial procurement, they satisfy the strict definition of a pilot model under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(4).
Step 2: Technical Documentation and Hypothesis-Driven Experimentation Protocols

To overcome the Tax Court's critique in Betz that proposals already contained known design parameters and that engineers merely performed standard calculations on existing data, AeroTherm institutes a mandatory three-stage documentation protocol within its PLM repository. First, before any CAD modeling begins on Subcomponent C-4, the lead chemical engineer executes a dated Pre-Design Technological Uncertainty Memorandum pursuant to IRC § 41(d)(1)(A). This document explicitly demonstrates why information available to AeroTherm—including prior customer projects, vendor literature, and ASME or EPA engineering standards—fails to establish the appropriate material composition and geometric clearance design of a rotary seal capable of maintaining leakage under hydrochloric acid vapor cycling. This directly severs Subcomponent C-4 from the IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) adaptation exclusion by proving that existing product architectures failed under these thermodynamic boundary conditions.

Second, for each iteration of Subcomponent C-4, engineers must maintain structured Process of Experimentation logs under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) that record a specific scientific hypothesis, such as positing that a silicon-carbide-coated Inconel 625 labyrinth seal with a radial thermal expansion relief slot will prevent galling during a thermal ramp. Engineers simultaneously archive all Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) and Finite Element Analysis (FEA) thermal stress simulation files comparing Alternative A (Inconel 625 labyrinth), Alternative B (Hastelloy C-276 braided ceramic rope seal), and Alternative C (pneumatically pressurized graphite face seal), including boundary condition inputs and failure modes. Third, the engineering team records empirical test bench data from the sacrificial pilot rigs in the Ohio laboratory, documenting why Alternatives A and B failed at cycle 420 due to acid condensation corrosion, and how Alternative C was modified to resolve the uncertainty. Post-installation EPA emissions testing at the customer's refinery is explicitly excluded from the R&D claim and categorized as non-qualifying quality control verification under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(6)(i) and (a)(7).
Step 3: Contractual Structuring to Prevent Funded Research Disqualification

To ensure the Gulf Coast refinery contract does not fail under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) as five of CPI's contracts did in Betz, AeroTherm's legal counsel revises the Master Equipment Supply Agreement prior to execution. To preserve substantial rights under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2), counsel strikes standard customer boilerplate stating that all drawings, designs, inventions, and technical data developed under the purchase order shall be the exclusive work-for-hire property of the buyer, replacing it with an explicit intellectual property bifurcation clause. That clause stipulates that AeroTherm retains sole and exclusive ownership, patent rights, and unrestricted commercial usage rights in all underlying research results, thermodynamic processes, catalyst formulations, rotary valve seal designs, and subcomponent inventions discovered or developed during the performance of the agreement, without any obligation to obtain the buyer's consent or pay any royalty or license fee, while granting the buyer only a non-exclusive operational license to use the delivered physical equipment at the designated facility. Furthermore, to satisfy the financial risk of failure standard under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1), AeroTherm structures the contract as a firm fixed-price agreement with strict performance guarantees tied explicitly to the technical success of the Subcomponent C-4 seal and catalyst matrix (99.95% halogenated VOC destruction with valve leakage), giving the customer the unconditional right to reject the equipment, withhold milestone payments, and demand full refund of progress payments if the technical specifications are not achieved through testing.
Step 4: Contemporaneous Time and Supply Cost Tracking

To satisfy IRC § 6001, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(d), and the Seventh Circuit's numerator rules in Little Sandy Coal, AeroTherm implements granular bi-weekly timekeeping and segregated Bill of Materials (BOM) accounting. AeroTherm configures its digital timesheet software so engineers and lab technicians log hours daily against five specific subcomponent task codes: 2026-RTO-100-EXP-C4-HYP for hypothesis formulation and alternative identification; 2026-RTO-100-EXP-C4-SIM for CFD/FEA simulation and iterative CAD modeling of seal alternatives; 2026-RTO-100-EXP-C4-PRO for hands-on fabrication and assembly of sacrificial benchtop test rigs constituting direct support under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B)(ii); 2026-RTO-100-EXP-C4-TST for empirical thermal-shock testing and failure analysis; and 2026-RTO-100-EXP-C4-SUP for direct first-line technical supervision of seal test data review. Supervisory hours are logged only when the Engineering Director actively evaluates test logs and directs parameter modifications, with mandatory text notes attached to each timesheet entry, while the Company President and COO are completely excluded from QRE claims unless they log contemporaneous, verifiable technical participation. Similarly, only raw materials (Inconel, Hastelloy, ceramic honeycombs, and test gases) requisitioned specifically for the three sacrificial lab test rigs under Job Code 2026-RTO-100-EXP-C4 are booked to the R&D Supplies General Ledger account, whereas all materials and subcontractor invoices for the commercial unit shipped to the customer are booked to standard Cost of Goods Sold (COGS) and excluded from the Form 6765 calculation.

body.text: Case Study 2: Specialized Process Automation and Environmental Control Systems Integrator (Subcontracted Fabrication and Client-Site Integration)
Baseline Scenario and Legal Pitfalls

ChemiClean Process Controls, LLC (ChemiClean), a United States domestic corporation and S corporation subsidiary group headquartered in Illinois (within the appellate venue of the Seventh Circuit, where Little Sandy Coal controls), engineers custom automated chemical scrubbing and closed-loop solvent recovery systems for semiconductor and pharmaceutical manufacturers. A semiconductor fabrication client ("FabCorp") contracts with ChemiClean to deliver a custom hydrogen peroxide and tetramethylammonium hydroxide (TMAH) vapor abatement and recovery system for its new cleanroom facility in Ireland ("The FabCorp Ireland Project").

Because ChemiClean previously engineered and installed a similar TMAH abatement system for FabCorp's Oregon facility two years prior, 75% of the Ireland project involves scaling flow rates by 15%, modifying piping layouts to fit the Ireland facility's ceiling grid, converting electrical schematics to European 50Hz/400V standards, and subcontracting local vessel fabrication. However, FabCorp's Ireland facility introduces a new ultra-pure water (UPW) reclamation mandate requiring ChemiClean to develop a novel Real-Time Spectroscopic Ion-Exchange Regeneration Algorithm and Membrane Control Loop (Subcomponent S-9) that prevents silica fouling at parts-per-trillion thresholds—something neither ChemiClean nor industry literature has ever achieved.

Furthermore, FabCorp's standard Engineering, Procurement, and Construction (EPC) contract pays ChemiClean on a monthly time-and-materials (T&M) invoice schedule with a 12% markup and states that ChemiClean may not disclose or utilize any technical innovations developed under the contract for any other semiconductor customer without paying FabCorp a 5% gross revenue royalty.

If ChemiClean claims the entire FabCorp Ireland Project on Form 6765 using retrospective estimates, the claim will suffer complete disallowance and Section 6662 negligence penalties under Betz across four distinct legal dimensions. First, scaling the prior Oregon design triggers the IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) adaptation exclusion, mirroring CPI's "M&W Ireland" project failure. Second, all subcontractor fabrication costs will be disqualified because, as in Betz, costs incurred to produce the final commercial product rather than a pilot model fail the Section 174 test, and no uncertainty is shown where a third party designs or builds a component to provided specifications without evidence of the taxpayer's own investigative activities. Third, the contract fails both prongs of the IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) funded research exclusion because T&M billing eliminates financial risk under Geosyntec, and the royalty and restriction clause destroys substantial rights under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3). Fourth, blending routine electrical and piping engineering with software experimentation causes the project to fail the 80% process of experimentation numerator test under Little Sandy Coal.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring Protocol
Step 1: Contractual Bifurcation and Amendment to Cure Funded Research Defects

Before commencing any engineering work, ChemiClean's tax counsel and commercial contracting team restructure the FabCorp engagement to eliminate the IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) funded research exclusion by splitting the commercial EPC contract from the R&D development agreement. ChemiClean bifurcates the scope into two separate legal instruments: Contract A (Commercial System Adaptation and Site Integration for $2.8 million on a T&M basis), which covers all scaling of the prior Oregon system, 50Hz electrical conversion, piping layout, third-party vessel subcontracting, and Ireland site commissioning, and which ChemiClean designates as 100% non-creditable adaptation under IRC § 41(d)(4)(B) and routine engineering; and Contract B (Development of the PPT Spectroscopic Ion-Exchange Control Module S-9 for a $650,000 conditional fixed price), which isolates the research and development of Subcomponent S-9 into a standalone Technology Development Rider.

To satisfy both the financial risk standard under Fairchild and Geosyntec and the substantial rights standard under Lockheed Martin and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d), payment of the $650,000 fee under Contract B is made expressly contingent upon Subcomponent S-9 demonstrating continuous silica breakthrough over a 500-hour validation trial in ChemiClean's Illinois testing facility; if Subcomponent S-9 fails to achieve this metric, ChemiClean receives zero compensation and absorbs 100% of its internal labor and prototype supply costs. Additionally, the 5% royalty and customer restriction clause is deleted in its entirety and replaced with a provision confirming that ChemiClean retains royalty-free, perpetual, non-exclusive substantial rights to commercialize the Subcomponent S-9 hardware and spectroscopic algorithms across all global clients.
Step 2: Project Governance and the 80% "Substantially All" Numerator Discipline

Because ChemiClean is located in Illinois (Seventh Circuit), its audit defense must strictly conform to the mathematical framework of Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), which Betz cited but did not need to apply to the 80% fraction. Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C), at least 80% of all research activities conducted on Subcomponent S-9 must constitute elements of a process of experimentation, expressed mathematically as:

To guarantee compliance with this fraction, ChemiClean establishes a dedicated project code (PROJ-S9-EXP) restricted exclusively to the spectroscopic control module and membrane regeneration loop. All routine data collection, customer status meetings, commercial procurement, and administrative project management are routed to Contract A (PROJ-IRE-ADAPT) so they do not pollute the denominator or dilute the 80% experimentation threshold of Subcomponent S-9.
Step 3: Technical Documentation of Software/Hardware Iterative Experimentation

To substantiate that Subcomponent S-9 underwent a rigorous scientific process of experimentation rather than routine control system programming, software and chemical process engineers link every code commit and chemometric simulation model in Git and Jira directly to an experimental hypothesis ticket under PROJ-S9-EXP. Each ticket contemporaneously documents the baseline capability uncertainty (explaining why standard PID conductivity loops cannot detect non-ionic colloidal silica breakthrough prior to membrane saturation), the competing mathematical and hardware alternatives evaluated (such as Raman spectroscopy neural-net deconvolution versus UV-persulfate oxidation coupled with differential laser refractometry), empirical test bench datasets injected with synthetic TMAH and silica foulants in the Illinois lab, and quantitative error-rate results driving each algorithmic and valve-timing iteration. In strict adherence to Betz's holdings that the production costs of final commercial units are not pilot-model supply QREs and that no uncertainty is shown where a third party designs or builds a component to provided specifications absent evidence of the taxpayer's own investigative activities, ChemiClean excludes all third-party vessel fabrication invoices from its QRE computation, claiming only in-house analytical sensor components and chemical reagents consumed in the Illinois laboratory test loop.
Step 4: Audit-Ready Substantiation File and Section 6662 Penalty Immunization

To prevent any assessment of accuracy-related penalties under IRC § 6662(a) and establish an unassailable evidentiary record—as well as a valid reasonable cause defense under IRC § 6664(c) should any technical dispute arise, consistent with George v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-10—ChemiClean institutionalizes quarterly substantiation governance. At the close of each quarter, ChemiClean's internal R&D Tax Committee compiles a Contemporaneous Substantiation Binder containing executed Contracts A and B, the Pre-Design Uncertainty Declaration contrasting Subcomponent S-9 against the prior Oregon facility schematics to prove non-adaptation, exported bi-weekly payroll and time-tracking logs verified by project managers at the time the sheets were submitted, lab test logs and Git commit histories, and a mathematical calculation of the 80% Little Sandy Coal fraction for Subcomponent S-9. Rather than engaging a study provider to create retrospective employee interview estimates, ChemiClean provides this complete contemporaneous dataset to an independent tax controversy attorney and CPA firm prior to filing Form 6765, ensuring full compliance with Treas. Reg. § 1.6664-4(c).

body.text: Section 5: Synthesis and Strategic Conclusions for U.S. Tax Practitioners

The Tax Court's decision in Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84, stands alongside Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), and Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113, as a watershed enforcement milestone in federal R&D tax credit litigation. The ruling confirms that custom-engineered-to-order manufacturing and industrial systems integration are not categorically barred from IRC § 41 eligibility, nor are reasonable allocations categorically prohibited when grounded in reliable records. However, Betz serves notice that the Tax Court will summarily reject credit claims built upon macro-system "pilot model" misclassifications, unsegregated business components that prevent shrinking-back analysis, commercial adaptation of prior designs, customer contracts that surrender substantial IP rights, and retrospective percentage estimates divorced from contemporaneous experimental documentation. Furthermore, the imposition of Section 6662 accuracy-related penalties despite the engagement of a specialized R&D study firm—sustained because the petitioners abandoned their reasonable cause defense and, alternatively, because their apparent reliance on that firm was inconsistent with ordinary business care and prudence, with negligence grounded in their failure to keep adequate records—demonstrates that pass-through shareholders and corporate taxpayers bear a non-delegable statutory duty under IRC § 6001 to maintain records sufficient to substantiate, at the component or subcomponent level, the uncertainty, investigative activities, and employee involvement underlying the credit; while the Court acknowledged that contemporaneous time-tracking records are not strictly required, vague or uncorroborated testimony will not suffice.
